subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: Find the equation of locus of a point P, if A = (2,3), B = (2,−3) and PA + PB = 8.

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this — say what you would do before squaring, and name the shape the locus turns out to be.

steps.label: Take the locus point
steps.margin_note: No mark of its own. Both fixed points share x = 2, so they sit one above the other — worth noticing before any algebra.
lines: Let P = (x, y) be a point on the locus.

recall.must_convey: That the moving point is named P = (x, y) and the fixed points are written down.
accept: let P be x comma y
take the locus point as P x y
P equals x comma y is on the locus
locus point ni P x y ga teesukovali
name the moving point P with coordinates x and y

steps.why: Every locus question starts the same way: the moving point gets coordinates, and the condition is then written in terms of those coordinates.
common_mistakes: Giving the moving point fixed numbers instead of (x, y).
Mixing up which points are fixed and which one moves.

steps.label: Write the given condition
steps.margin_note: First mark. Move one distance across BEFORE squaring, so only one square root is ever squared at a time. The line is then arranged with the surviving root alone on one side.

recall.must_convey: That PA is isolated as 8 − PB and squared, giving 16PB = 64 + PB² − PA².
accept: shift P B across and square so P A squared equals sixty four plus P B squared minus sixteen P B
isolate one distance first then square both sides
write P A as eight minus P B and square it
oka distance ni separate chesi square cheyyali
rearrange to get sixteen P B on one side

steps.why: A sum of two distances cannot be squared directly — squaring PA + PB gives a cross term. Isolating one distance first is what keeps the algebra finite.
common_mistakes: Squaring PA + PB = 8 directly and being left with a 2·PA·PB cross term.
Squaring only one side of PA = 8 − PB.

steps.label: Substitute the distances
steps.margin_note: Second mark, and the moment the question becomes easy. Because both fixed points share x = 2, the (x−2)² terms are identical and cancel outright, leaving a difference of two squares in y alone.

recall.must_convey: That substituting makes the (x−2)² terms cancel, and the difference of squares in y gives 4PB = 16 + 3y.
accept: the x minus two squared terms cancel and the y difference of squares gives four a b
substitute and use a plus b whole squared minus a minus b whole squared equals four a b
both x terms are the same so they cancel leaving four P B equals sixteen plus three y
x terms cancel avuthaayi, y lo difference of squares vasthundi
reduce it to four P B equals sixteen plus three y

steps.why: PA² − PB² is a difference of two squares, so the y-terms collapse by (a+b)² − (a−b)² = 4ab and the whole line drops to the first degree.
common_mistakes: Expanding both brackets in full and losing a sign instead of cancelling them.

steps.label: Simplify to the locus
steps.margin_note: The last two marks. Square once more to clear the surviving root, then collect. The x² and y² coefficients come out DIFFERENT and both positive — what identifies the locus as an ellipse.

recall.must_convey: That squaring again and collecting gives 16x² + 7y² − 64x − 48 = 0.
accept: square again and collect to get sixteen x squared plus seven y squared minus sixty four x minus forty eight equals zero
the ninety six y cancels and sixteen y squared minus nine y squared is seven y squared
square both sides once more and simplify to the ellipse
malli square chesi simplify chesthe ellipse vasthundi
the locus is an ellipse

steps.why: The locus of a point whose distances to two fixed points add to a constant is an ellipse with those points as foci, so unequal positive coefficients on x² and y² are the expected finish.
common_mistakes: Forgetting that 96y appears on both sides and cancels.
Multiplying only the first bracket by 16.
